g10-biology-ub3-t1.overview: Life is a water story: your cells are ~70% water, your blood is ~90% plasma-water, and every reaction in you happens in aqueous solution. Water's polarity — one slightly-negative oxygen, two slightly-positive hydrogens — makes it the universal solvent, the temperature buffer, the transport fluid and the lubricant of biology.
objectives: Explain water's polarity and hydrogen bonding from its structure
List water's properties: solvent, cohesion/adhesion, high heat capacity, latent heat, density anomaly
Connect each property to a biological example
Describe the water cycle's biological role and safe-water basics
g10-biology-ub3-t1.simple: Oxygen hogs the shared electrons in H₂O, so one side of the molecule is slightly negative (O) and the other slightly positive (H) — a POLAR molecule, like a tiny magnet. Magnets attract magnets: water molecules stick to each other (hydrogen bonds) → cohesion; they stick to other polar things → adhesion; and they surround ions and polar molecules, dissolving them → the universal solvent. Those same weak bonds make water resist temperature change (high heat capacity — oceans and your body stay stable), need lots of energy to evaporate (sweat cooling), and make ICE FLOAT (insulating lakes so fish survive winter). Life chose water; nothing cheap does all this at once.
g10-biology-ub3-t1.detailed:
Structure → polarity: O shares electrons with 2 H at 104.5°; oxygen's higher electronegativity pulls the bonding electrons its way → partial charges (δ⁻ on O, δ⁺ on H). Result: a dipole. Adjacent molecules attract δ⁺ to δ⁻ = HYDROGEN BOND — individually weak (~5% of a covalent bond) but collectively massive (a water molecule makes up to 4).

Property 1 — solvent: polar water shells ions (hydration spheres: δ⁺ H's around Cl⁻, δ⁻ O around Na⁺) → dissolves salts, sugars, amino acids — 'aqueous' = life's reaction medium. Blood plasma (~92% water) carries nutrients/hormones/wastes; cytoplasm is water-based; hydrophobic (non-polar: oils) DON'T dissolve — hence cell membranes need special transport.

Property 2 — cohesion/adhesion → transport: H-bonded water columns resist tension (transpiration pull in xylem — links to Unit 2), capillary action in soil and tiny vessels, surface tension (insects walk on water; water striders).

Property 3 — thermal stability: high specific heat (4.18 J/g·°C — H-bonds absorb heat before molecules fly apart): oceans moderate climate, organisms resist temperature swings. High latent heat of vaporisation: evaporating 1 g sweat removes ~2.4 kJ — the body's air conditioning. Solid ice LESS dense than liquid (open H-bond lattice): lakes freeze top-down, aquatic life survives winter; icebergs float.

Property 4 — reactivity: water isn't inert: hydrolysis (adding H₂O breaks polymers — digestion), condensation (removing H₂O builds them), photosynthesis's electron source (photolysis), respiration's product. Water participates in the very reactions that define metabolism.

Water and health (Ethiopian context): ~10% of global disease burden links to unsafe water/sanitation; ORS (oral rehydration solution — glucose+salts in clean water) saves diarrhoea deaths cheaply (the WHO formula: ~1 L water + 6 tsp sugar + ½ tsp salt); boiling/treatment (lake and well water), the role of water in food safety (cholera outbreaks). Safe water is biology as public policy.

keyTerms.def: Uneven charge in H₂O — δ⁻ oxygen, δ⁺ hydrogens.
Weak δ⁺H–δ⁻ attraction between water molecules — collective strength.
Dissolves polar/ionic substances via hydration shells.
Water-loving (polar) / water-fearing (non-polar, e.g. oils).
Water-water / water-surface attraction — enables xylem transport.
Resists temperature change — climate and body stability.
Evaporation removes big heat — sweating cools.
Ice floats — open lattice; lakes freeze top-down.
Water breaks / water removed to build biomolecules.
Oral rehydration solution — water + salt + sugar saves diarrhoea lives.

workedExamples.problem: Explain, using polarity, why NaCl dissolves in water but oil does not.
workedExamples.substitution: NaCl: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; water's δ⁺ H's cluster around Cl⁻, δ⁻ O's around Na⁺ — hydration shells pry ions apart. Oil: non-polar hydrocarbons — no charges for water to grab; water prefers bonding to itself, squeezing oil out (phase separation).
workedExamples.answer: Water dissolves charged/polar things by ion-dipole attraction; oils offer nothing to attract — they're excluded.

workedExamples.problem: Coastal cities stay cooler by day and warmer by night than inland deserts. Which water property explains this?
workedExamples.substitution: Water absorbs/releases enormous heat with little temperature change (H-bonds soak energy); oceans act as thermal buffers — daytime heat sinks into sea, night-time it leaks back.
workedExamples.calculation: Sand: low heat capacity → scorching days, freezing nights.
workedExamples.answer: Water's heat capacity moderates temperature — for cities AND for your cells staying at 37 °C.

workedExamples.problem: A child has severe watery diarrhoea. Explain why plain water isn't enough and what ORS does, biologically.
workedExamples.substitution: Diarrhoea loses water AND salts (Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻); plain water lacks Na⁺/glucose → poor absorption, dilutes remaining salts (dangerous hyponatraemia). ORS glucose drives Na⁺ (and water by osmosis) absorption via co-transport in the gut; salts restore gradients.
workedExamples.calculation: WHO-ORS: ~75 mmol/L Na⁺, 75 mmol/L glucose, 1 L water.
workedExamples.answer: ORS turns the gut's glucose-Na⁺ co-transport into a water pump — cheap biology saving millions of lives.

workedExamples.problem: Why does a frozen lake NOT freeze solid, and why does that matter for fish?
workedExamples.substitution: Below 4 °C water's H-bonds lock into an OPEN hexagonal lattice → ice is ~9% less dense → floats. The floating layer INSULATES the water below (4 °C at depth — water's densest), so the lake bottom stays liquid.
workedExamples.calculation: If ice sank: bottom-up freezing → lakes solid in winter.
workedExamples.answer: Floating ice = a thermal lid — aquatic ecosystems survive cold seasons because water expands on freezing.

workedExamples.problem: Link water's cohesion to a plant process from Unit 2: how does a sunflower lift 2 L of water a day to its leaves?
workedExamples.substitution: Evaporation from leaf mesophyll creates tension; H-bonded water molecules pull as a continuous chain (cohesion) through xylem; adhesion braces the column against vessel walls; root uptake replaces the volume.
workedExamples.calculation: No pump needed — the sun evaporates, the water column follows.
workedExamples.answer: Water's H-bond teamwork turns leaf evaporation into a whole-plant elevator.

commonMistakes: Saying water is 'non-polar because it's neutral overall' — net charge zero, but CHARGE SEPARATION (dipole) is everything.
Calling a hydrogen bond a covalent bond — it's a weak inter-molecular attraction, not shared-electron bonding.
Thinking ice is denser than water — it's LESS dense (open lattice) — that's why it floats.
Believing sweat cools by being cold — it cools by EVAPORATING (latent heat); humidity blocks evaporation (muggy heat = dangerous).
Saying 'water dissolves everything' — it dissolves polar/ionic things; oils and gases poorly.
ORS confusion: giving only water or only salty water — the GLUCOSE-SODIUM co-transport is the mechanism; both are needed.
Forgetting water REACTS (hydrolysis/condensation) — it's a metabolic participant, not just a solvent.
applications: Human thermoregulation: sweating (latent heat) + blood-water heat distribution — highland vs lowland work rates.
Agriculture: soil water's cohesion/adhesion holds moisture in capillary pores; wilting point when roots can't pull it free.
Public health: ORS for diarrhoea (Ethiopian HEW networks promote it), water treatment (chlorination, boiling), WASH programs.
Aquaculture & lakes: density anomaly protects Lake Tana/Abaya life through cold nights.
Food preservation: drying removes water → microbes can't run aqueous metabolism (injera batter, dried vegetables, berbere).
Cooking science: water's heat capacity = even boiling; oil's lower capacity + higher max temp = frying.
g10-biology-ub3-t1.summary: H₂O's polarity → hydrogen bonds → the property package: universal solvent (hydration shells), cohesion/adhesion (transport, capillarity), high heat capacity + latent heat (climate and body stability, sweating), ice floating (aquatic winter survival), and metabolic reactivity (hydrolysis/condensation, photolysis). Life's medium, thermostat, highway and lubricant — and ORS proves knowing water's biology saves lives.

pairs.q: Why does oil float on water AND refuse to mix?
pairs.a: Non-polar oil can't H-bond; water molecules prefer each other, excluding oil — and oil is less dense, so it rides on top.

pairs.q: Why is humid heat more dangerous than dry heat at the same temperature?
pairs.a: Sweat cools by evaporating; humid air is already full of water, so evaporation stalls and the body overheats.

pairs.q: Why can fish live under a frozen lake?
pairs.a: Ice floats and insulates; water below stays liquid at ~4 °C (its densest point).

questions.q: Water molecules attract each other because water is:
questions.explanation: The dipole (δ⁺H, δ⁻O) enables hydrogen bonding between molecules.

questions.q: The weak attraction between water's δ⁺H and a neighbour's δ⁻O is a ____ bond.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds — individually weak, collectively powerful.

questions.q: Ice floats because:
options: H-bonds form an open lattice making it less dense
questions.explanation: The crystalline lattice spaces molecules apart — solid water is ~9% less dense.

questions.q: How does sweating cool the body — name the property involved.
questions.answer: latent heat evaporation|evaporation removes heat|high heat of vaporisation
questions.explanation: Evaporating sweat absorbs ~2.4 kJ/g of body heat — water's high latent heat.

questions.q: Water dissolves oils well because both are liquids.
questions.explanation: Like dissolves like: polar water excludes non-polar oils.

questions.q: ORS works because glucose drives absorption of ____ ions (name/symbol).
questions.explanation: Na⁺-glucose co-transport pulls salt, and water follows osmotically.

questions.q: Why does a lake freeze from the TOP down instead of the bottom?
questions.answer: ice floats insulates|4 degrees densest|cold water on top
questions.explanation: Ice is less dense → stays on top; below, water sinks to 4 °C (densest) — the surface freezes first.

questions.q: The reaction that BREAKS polymers by adding water is:
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis = water splits bonds; condensation joins them losing water.

questions.q: Evaporating sweat removes ~2.4 kJ per gram. How many kJ does 50 g of sweat removal cool? (kJ)
questions.explanation: 50 × 2.4 = 120 kJ — a workout's heat dumped.

g10-biology-ub3-t2.overview: Beyond water, organisms run on a handful of ions: sodium and potassium fire nerves, calcium builds bones and clots blood, iron carries oxygen in haemoglobin, iodine loads thyroid hormones, phosphate links DNA and powers ATP. Tiny amounts, enormous jobs — and the right balance is life itself.
objectives: Name major biological ions and their functions
Link ion roles to symptoms of deficiency/excess
Explain ions in osmoregulation and nerve impulses (Na⁺/K⁺)
Describe mineral ions in plants (N, P, K, Mg, Ca, S sources and roles)
Relate electrolyte balance to health (ORS, sweating, cramps)
g10-biology-ub3-t2.simple: Ions are charged atoms floating in body fluids — electrolytes. Sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) run the nerve-impulse pump (every thought is a Na⁺/K⁺ wave); chloride (Cl⁻) keeps electrical balance; calcium (Ca²⁺) builds bone/shells, clots blood and triggers muscle squeeze; iron (Fe²⁺/³⁺) sits in haemoglobin and carries O₂; iodine (I⁻) loads thyroid hormones; phosphate (PO₄³⁻) is DNA's backbone, ATP's energy and bone's hardness. Plants need their own set from soil: nitrate for proteins, magnesium for chlorophyll, phosphate for energy. Deficiency = symptoms: no iron → anaemia, no iodine → goitre, no nitrate → yellow stunted crops.
g10-biology-ub3-t2.detailed:
Animals/humans — the ion roster:
• Na⁺ (extracellular fluid): osmotic balance, nerve impulses, muscle; lost in sweat; excess → hypertension.
• K⁺ (intracellular): nerve conduction, heart rhythm; deficiency → weakness/arrhythmia.
• Ca²⁺: bones/teeth (hydroxyapatite), blood clotting cascade, muscle contraction, nerve transmission; deficiency → cramps/tetany, rickets/osteoporosis.
• Cl⁻: stomach HCl (digestion + pathogen kill), osmotic balance.
• Fe²⁺: haemoglobin's oxygen carrier (and myoglobin); deficiency → anaemia (fatigue, pallor).
• I⁻: thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4/T3) — metabolism control; deficiency → goitre, cretinism in children.
• PO₄³⁻: ATP, DNA/RNA backbone, phospholipids, bone mineral.
• HCO₃⁻: blood pH buffer (with CO₂).

Ions as signals: the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in per ATP → resting membrane potential (~−70 mV). A stimulus opens Na⁺ channels (influx → depolarisation = the action potential), then K⁺ channels (repolarisation). Nerve impulses ARE moving ion gradients. Muscle contraction: Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum slides actin/myosin. Heart rhythm: K⁺ balance is literally life-or-death (why diarrhoea kills children — electrolyte loss).

Plants' mineral ions (from soil solution): N (nitrate NH₄⁺): amino acids/proteins, chlorophyll, nucleic acids — deficiency: stunted, yellow OLD leaves (mobile). P (phosphate): ATP, nucleic acids, root growth — stunted, purple-tinged. K (potassium): enzyme activation, stomata guard-cell pumping — scorched leaf margins, weak stems. Mg: chlorophyll's central atom — interveinal chlorosis (old leaves first). Ca: cell-wall calcium pectate — tip/edge die-back, bitter pit in fruit (immobile). S: cysteine/methionine amino acids — young-leaf yellowing. Legumes + Rhizobium fix N; fertilisers (urea, NPS) replace harvest losses.

Balance & health: electrolytes measured in blood panels (Na⁺ 135-145 mmol/L); sweating loses Na⁺/Cl⁻ → cramps/hyponatraemia if replaced with plain water only (marathon lesson); ORS restores Na⁺/glucose; iodised-salt programs (Ethiopia's universal salt iodisation cut goitre rates); kidney osmoregulation (links to Unit 5 urinary system).

keyTerms.def: Ion in body fluid carrying charge (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻…).
3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in per ATP — nerve resting potential.
Na⁺-influx wave along a nerve — an electrical impulse.
Fe²⁺ binds O₂ — anaemia when iron short.
Swollen thyroid from iodine deficiency.
Ca-phosphate crystal — bone/teeth hardness.
Plant N source — proteins/chlorophyll; deficiency yellows old leaves.
Chlorophyll's centre atom — interveinal chlorosis when lacking.
Kidney/skin control of water-ion balance.

workedExamples.problem: A long-distance runner drinks only plain water through a 3-hour sweaty race and collapses confused. Diagnosis with ion logic?
workedExamples.substitution: Sweat removes salt; replacing ONLY water dilutes remaining blood Na⁺ below 135 mmol/L → water shifts into brain cells (osmosis) → swelling, confusion, seizures.
workedExamples.calculation: Prevention: electrolyte drinks/ORS during endurance events.
workedExamples.answer: Dilutional hyponatraemia — plain water alone can be dangerous when salt is sweated out.

workedExamples.problem: Match each symptom to its missing ion: (a) fatigue + pale skin, low O₂ capacity; (b) swollen neck thyroid; (c) muscle cramps + weak bones; (d) stunted maize with purple-tinged old leaves.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) Fe²⁺ (haemoglobin). (b) I⁻ (thyroxine). (c) Ca²⁺ (bone/muscle). (d) P (phosphate — purple = anthocyanin buildup when energy metabolism stalls).
workedExamples.calculation: Each ion has a signature shortage.
workedExamples.answer: Iron, iodine, calcium, phosphate — four ions, four stories.

workedExamples.problem: Explain, step by step, how a nerve impulse travels as an ion event.
workedExamples.substitution: (1) Rest: pump keeps Na⁺ out, K⁺ in, membrane −70 mV. (2) Stimulus opens Na⁺ channels → Na⁺ floods in → inside turns positive (depolarisation). (3) The voltage change opens the NEXT channel segment — wave travels. (4) K⁺ channels open → K⁺ exits → repolarisation. (5) Pump resets.
workedExamples.answer: A nerve impulse is a self-propagating Na⁺/K⁺ redistribution — electricity made of ions.

workedExamples.problem: An Ethiopian highland farmer's teff shows yellowing between the veins on LOWER leaves while the top stays green. Which ion, and why the pattern?
workedExamples.substitution: Mg²⁺ is chlorophyll's central atom AND phloem-mobile: the plant pulls Mg from old leaves to feed new growth → old leaves yellow between veins (veins keep transport tissue green longer); top growth stays green by cannibalising the bottom.
workedExamples.calculation: Fix: Epsom salts (MgSO₄) or lime-adjusted soil (high-P soils can lock Mg out).
workedExamples.answer: Magnesium deficiency — mobile-nutrient pattern: old leaves sacrificed first.

commonMistakes: Saying nerves conduct 'electricity like a wire' — it's ION movement (Na⁺/K⁺), not electron flow.
Confusing Na⁺/K⁺ pump direction: 3 Na⁺ OUT, 2 K⁺ IN (per ATP).
Thinking calcium is only bones — clotting, muscle contraction and nerve signalling need it too.
Attributing goitre to 'too much salt' — it's iodine deficiency (salt is just the delivery vehicle for iodisation).
Believing plants 'eat' fertiliser as food — ions are raw materials for building (N for amino acids), not energy sources.
Mixing deficiency leaf patterns: mobile (N, P, K, Mg) → OLD leaves first; immobile (Ca, Fe, S) → YOUNG leaves.
Drinking only water during heavy sweating — replacing fluid without salt causes hyponatraemia.
Calling phosphate just 'a fertiliser ion' — it's ATP, DNA backbone and bone mineral simultaneously.
applications: ORS and electrolyte powders for diarrhoea — Ethiopia's HEW/health-post staple against child dehydration.
Universal salt iodisation — national program that slashed goitre/cretinism rates.
Blood panels (Na⁺/K⁺/Ca²⁺) in every hospital — diagnosis by ion balance.
Fertiliser blending (NPS, urea) for teff/wheat — replacing harvested ions; Ethiopia's soil-restoration agenda.
Legume rotation (fava beans, lentils) fixing N via Rhizobium — natural ion farming.
Sports drinks & cramp prevention — replacing sweat Na⁺/K⁺.
g10-biology-ub3-t2.summary: Ions = body's electrolytes: Na⁺/K⁺ (nerves, osmotic balance), Ca²⁺ (bone, clotting, contraction), Cl⁻ (HCl), Fe²⁺ (O₂ transport), I⁻ (thyroid), PO₄³⁻ (ATP/DNA/bone), HCO₃⁻ (pH). Plants need N, P, K, Mg, Ca, S — deficiency patterns reveal mobility. Nerve impulses are ion waves; balance is life (ORS, iodised salt, fertilisers).

pairs.q: Why do marathoners take salt tabs, not just water?
pairs.a: Sweat loses Na⁺; plain water dilutes blood sodium → hyponatraemia (brain-cell swelling).

pairs.q: Why do legume fields feed the next cereal crop?
pairs.a: Rhizobium bacteria fix N₂ into ammonium — the field gains nitrate ions for free.

pairs.q: Why is iodised salt a public-health tool?
pairs.a: Iodine deficiency causes goitre/cretinism; salting the salt reaches every kitchen cheaply.

questions.q: The ion at the centre of chlorophyll is:
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ sits in chlorophyll's ring — without it, no green.

questions.q: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 sodium ions ____ and 2 potassium ions ____ per ATP.
questions.explanation: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in — builds the resting potential.

questions.q: A goitre (swollen thyroid) indicates deficiency of:
questions.explanation: I⁻ is needed for thyroxine; the gland enlarges trying to catch any iodine.

questions.q: Why does iron deficiency cause fatigue?
questions.explanation: Fe²⁺ carries O₂ in haemoglobin; less iron → less oxygen to mitochondria → less ATP → fatigue.

questions.q: Nerve impulses travel as electrons moving through the axon like a copper wire.
questions.explanation: They are ion waves (Na⁺/K⁺ fluxes across membrane), not electron flow.

questions.q: Plant nitrate deficiency first shows as:
questions.explanation: N is mobile — pulled from old leaves to new growth → general old-leaf yellowing + stunting.

questions.q: The phosphate-containing energy currency of cells is ____.
questions.explanation: ATP — adenosine triphosphate; its bonds power cellular work.

questions.q: Explain why severe diarrhoea can kill a child even if they drink plenty of plain water.
questions.explanation: Diarrhoea drains Na⁺/K⁺/HCO₃⁻; plain water dilutes what remains → nerve/heart function and pH collapse — ORS (salt+glucose) is the fix.

questions.q: Calcium's roles include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: O₂ transport is iron's job (haemoglobin); Ca²⁺ does clotting, contraction, bone.

g10-biology-ub3-t3.overview: Carbon's four-handed bonding builds life's four big molecule families: carbohydrates (sugars/starches — quick energy), lipids (fats/oils — dense energy + membranes), proteins (amino-acid machines — structure, catalysis, transport) and nucleic acids (DNA/RNA — information). This lesson covers their monomers, bonds, tests and jobs.
objectives: List the four biomolecule classes with monomer and bond names
Classify carbohydrates: mono-, di-, polysaccharides with examples
Describe lipid structure (glycerol + fatty acids) and functions
Explain protein structure levels and enzyme role
Perform/interpret biochemical tests (iodine, Benedict's, biuret, emulsion, grease spot)
g10-biology-ub3-t3.simple: Carbon makes 4 bonds → endless chains → life's molecules. CARBOHYDRATES = sugar units: glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, instant energy), sucrose/lactose (two sugars), starch/glycogen/cellulose (long chains — storage or structure). LIPIDS = glycerol + fatty-acid chains: fats (solid, animal) and oils (liquid, plant — sesame/olive), membranes, hormone carriers, long-term energy (2× energy per gram of sugar). PROTEINS = amino-acid chains folded into machines: enzymes, haemoglobin, muscle, keratin, antibodies. NUCLEIC ACIDS = nucleotide chains: DNA stores the instructions, RNA carries them out. Build them by condensation (lose water), break them by hydrolysis (add water) — and kitchen chemistry tests reveal which is on the plate.
g10-biology-ub3-t3.detailed:
Carbohydrates: C:H:O ≈ 1:2:1. Monosaccharides: glucose (energy currency of cells), fructose (fruit), ribose (RNA); ring forms. Disaccharides: maltose (glucose+glucose), sucrose (glucose+fructose — cane/beet sugar), lactose (glucose+galactose — milk). Polysaccharides: starch (amylose helix + amylopectin branched — plant storage: teff, potato, enset), glycogen (animal storage — liver/muscle, highly branched), cellulose (β-glucose straight chains H-bonded into fibres — plant walls, our 'fibre' we can't digest but gut bacteria partly ferment), chitin (N-containing — insect exoskeletons, fungal walls). Reducing sugars (glucose, maltose, lactose) give positive Benedict's; sucrose doesn't.

Lipids: Triglycerides = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (ester bonds). Saturated (no C=C, animal fats, solid) vs unsaturated (C=C kinks, plant oils, liquid — healthier profile). Functions: energy store (39 kJ/g vs 17 kJ/g for carbs — compact, anhydrous), insulation (Ethiopian highland herders' subcutaneous fat), membranes (phospholipid bilayer), waterproofing (leaf cuticle, fur oils), hormones (steroids: sex hormones, cortisol), vitamin carriers (A, D, E, K). Emulsion test (ethanol + water → milky) detects them.

Proteins: 20 amino acids (amine + carboxyl + variable R group) joined by PEPTIDE bonds → polypeptide. Structure levels: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix/β-sheet — H-bonds), tertiary (3D fold — R-group interactions), quaternary (multiple chains — haemoglobin's 4). Fold = function; denaturation (heat/pH) unfolds → loses function (fried egg can't un-fry). Roles: enzymes (catalysts), transport (haemoglobin), structure (keratin, collagen, actin/myosin), defence (antibodies), hormones (insulin), buffers. Biuret test (blue → violet) detects peptide bonds.

Nucleic acids: nucleotides = sugar (ribose/deoxyribose) + phosphate + base (DNA: A,T,G,C; RNA: A,U,G,C). DNA double helix (H-bonded base pairs A-T, G-C) stores genes; RNA (single strand) executes: mRNA (message), tRNA (adaptor), rRNA (ribosome). ATP = a nucleotide derivative — the energy link between families.

Bond chemistry: condensation (monomer–monomer → dimer + H₂O: glycosidic, peptide, ester, phosphodiester) vs hydrolysis (add H₂O to break — digestion's job).

Plant storage / animal storage / plant-wall fibre.
Glycerol + 3 fatty acids — fat/oil.
No C=C (solid fats) / with C=C kinks (liquid oils).

formulas.name: Glucose
formulas.example: Teff starch is hundreds of glucose units linked.

formulas.name: Energy density
formulas.when: Why animals store fat, not sugar.
formulas.example: 1 kg fat ≈ 2.3 kg glycogen (which also drags ~3× its weight in water).

workedExamples.problem: Describe how you would test a crushed teff sample, an oil seed (nug), and a piece of meat for their main biomolecule — name test, reagent, positive result.
workedExamples.substitution: Teff + iodine solution → blue-BLACK (starch). Nug: crush in ethanol, add water → milky emulsion (oil). Meat + biuret (NaOH + CuSO₄) → violet (protein).
workedExamples.calculation: Benedict's on teff (after boiling) would also show reducing sugars from partial starch breakdown.
workedExamples.answer: Iodine-black, emulsion-milky, biuret-violet — three foods, three positive tests.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why cellulose and starch — both glucose polymers — behave so differently (one digests easily, one is fibre).
workedExamples.substitution: Starch: α-glucose helical/branched — our amylase fits α-glycosidic bonds → glucose released. Cellulose: β-glucose straight chains cross-H-bonded into tough microfibrils — humans lack cellulase (gut microbes partly ferment it = fibre benefit).
workedExamples.calculation: Ruminants (Ethiopian cattle) host cellulase-making microbes — they digest grass.
workedExamples.answer: Bond geometry decides: α = digestible storage; β = structural fibre needing microbial help.

workedExamples.problem: A patient's enzymes stop working after a high fever. Explain with protein structure.
workedExamples.substitution: Heat breaks the weak H-bonds/interactions holding tertiary structure → active-site shape distorts → substrate no longer fits (lock-and-key broken) → catalysis stops. Some proteins refold on cooling; prolonged fever = permanent damage.
workedExamples.calculation: Same reason cooking softens food — denatured proteins digest easier.
workedExamples.answer: Fever denatures enzymes — the 3D shape that IS the function collapses.

workedExamples.problem: Compare energy storage: why do migratory birds and hibernating animals load fat rather than glycogen?
workedExamples.substitution: Fat: 39 kJ/g, stored anhydrous (light, compact). Glycogen: 17 kJ/g AND binds ~3 g water per gram — heavy and bulky.
workedExamples.calculation: For flight, every gram counts — fat wins on mass-specific energy.
workedExamples.answer: Fat is the high-density, dry battery — glycogen is the wet, heavy one.

workedExamples.problem: Show how ONE molecule family links to the others: trace glucose → starch → (digestion) → glucose → respiration → ATP, and name the bond types broken/formed.
workedExamples.substitution: Glucose → starch by α-glycosidic bonds (condensation, teff stores it). Digestion hydrolyses (amylase + H₂O) → glucose absorbed. Respiration oxidises glucose → ATP (phosphoanhydride energy). ATP itself is a nucleotide derivative — nucleic-acid chemistry.
workedExamples.calculation: Water built it, water breaks it, oxygen cashes it.
workedExamples.answer: Carbs, bonds, hydrolysis and nucleotide energy — one continuous story.

commonMistakes: Saying 'sugar = bad' — glucose is the cell's preferred fuel; the issue is quantity/refined excess.
Calling all fats 'bad lipids' — membranes, hormones and vitamin transport REQUIRE lipids; unsaturated oils are the healthy profile.
Confusing starch and cellulose 'both plants so same' — α vs β linkages make one food and one fibre.
Benedict's test needs HEATING (blue → brick-red); iodine does not (blue-black instantly).
Saying enzymes are 'used up' — they catalyse repeatedly; they denature eventually but aren't consumed.
Believing proteins' job is only muscle — enzymes, antibodies, transport, hormones are all proteins.
Thinking DNA is 'in the nucleus doing energy work' — DNA stores information; ATP (a relative) handles energy.
Calling lactose a plant sugar — it's the MILK disaccharide (glucose + galactose); adults lacking lactase get intolerance.
applications: Nutrition science: teff = complex carb + protein + iron; nug/niger seed = lipid; lentils/fava = protein — the Ethiopian plate is a biomolecule map.
Food testing in labs and quality control (adulterated honey = sugar profile tests).
Lactose intolerance (lactase persistence genetics) — why milk handling differs across populations.
Cooking chemistry: denaturation (egg, injera batter setting), Maillard browning (proteins + sugars).
Textiles: cotton = cellulose, silk/wool = protein — fibre identification by burn/chemical tests.
Biofuels: oils (lipids) → biodiesel; starch/sugar → ethanol fermentation.
g10-biology-ub3-t3.summary: Four families, four monomers: carbs (monosaccharides, glycosidic bonds — glucose/starch/cellulose), lipids (glycerol + fatty acids, ester bonds — energy/membranes), proteins (amino acids, peptide bonds — 4 structure levels, enzymes), nucleic acids (nucleotides, phosphodiester — DNA/RNA). Condensation builds, hydrolysis breaks. Tests: iodine→starch, Benedict's(heat)→reducing sugar, biuret→protein, emulsion→lipid.

pairs.q: Ethanol + water shaken with ground peanut →?

questions.q: The monomer of proteins is the:
questions.explanation: 20 amino acids → peptide bonds → polypeptides.

questions.q: Iodine solution turning blue-black proves the presence of:
questions.explanation: Iodine slips into starch's helix → blue-black.

questions.q: The bond linking two amino acids is a ____ bond.
questions.explanation: Peptide bond (condensation, −H₂O).

questions.q: Why do humans get no energy from cellulose even though it is made of glucose?
questions.explanation: Our enzymes can't hydrolyse β-glycosidic bonds — only microbes (ruminants, our gut partly) can.

questions.q: Which lipid property makes it the best long-term energy store?
questions.explanation: Double the energy per gram of carbs, without water weight.

questions.q: Enzymes are consumed in the reactions they catalyse.
questions.explanation: Catalysts emerge unchanged — one enzyme molecule works thousands of times.

questions.q: The test reagent that turns violet with proteins is ____.
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent (alkaline CuSO₄) + peptide bonds → violet.

questions.q: DNA's building blocks are:
questions.explanation: Nucleotides: sugar + phosphate + base (A/T/G/C).

questions.q: A fever 'cooks' an enzyme. Use structure terms to explain what stops working.
questions.explanation: Heat breaks weak bonds holding tertiary structure → active site distorts → substrate no longer fits.

questions.q: Pick the correct protein structure hierarchy:
questions.explanation: Sequence → local folds → 3D → multi-chain assembly.
